newsitem.title: USA: Prosecution urges death for Oklahoma City bomber.
newsitem.headline: Prosecution urges death for Oklahoma City bomber.

text.p: The prosecution in the Oklahoma City bombing trial on Wednesday began its attempt to persuade the jury to condemn convicted bomber Timothy McVeigh to death, saying it was the only punishment to fit such a heinous crime.

Two days after McVeigh was found guilty of murder and conspiracy by the same jury, prosecutor Pat Ryan said McVeigh had meticulously planned the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah Building that killed 168 people.

"We will ask you to return a verdict of death, the only verdict that justly fits this crime," a solemn Ryan said in the opening statement of the trial's penalty phase, expected to be the most emotional and heart-rending part of the trial.
The Gulf War Army veteran wanted to "make sure that maximum impact was caused by his bomb. He wanted the blood to flow in the streets of America," Ryan said.

"It would be easy to think of this as one mass murder. Don't. It's 168 people, all individual, all different. All of them had family, all of them had friends. One hundred and sixty-eight people all died a violent and frightening death," Ryan, the U.S. Attorney for Oklahoma City, said.
McVeigh killed husbands, wives, grandchildren and parents, and also three unborn children since three of the victims were pregnant, he said.
Several relatives of bombing victims in the court wiped their eyes. Before the session began, two prosecutors spoke to the relatives, warning them how emotional the day would be.
McVeigh, convicted of 11 counts of conspiracy, bombing and first-degree murder, showed no emotion.

Prosecutors say he is a right-wing fanatic driven to bomb the building by hatred for the U.S. government. Over the next week, the jury of seven men and five women will be asked to decide whether he will be executed or put in prison for life.

They will hear evidence from witnesses for both sides, then decide if the aggravating factors outweigh the mitigating ones. Many legal analysts said the defence faces a daunting task to persuade the jurors to spare McVeigh's life.

Federal Judge Richard Matsch told the jury they must wait to hear all of the evidence before making any decisions. "Your role is to be the conscience of the community in making a moral judgment about the value of a specific life," he said.

The prosecution plans to call about 40 witnesses including survivors, victims' relatives and rescue workers to testify about the horror of the bombing. Later, the defence will call its own witnesses to try to show mitigating factors such as McVeigh's good conduct when he served in the Army.

Ryan listed seven aggravating factors that the prosecution says justifies the death penalty for McVeigh, including premeditation, the deaths of law enforcement officers, the large number of people killed, maimed or disfigured and the impact on survivors or relatives of victims.
He warned the jurors the information he would give them would be "difficult for us to present (and) painful for you to hear."

He said McVeigh carefully planned and executed the bombing, hatching the plan "months and months" beforehand. He said McVeigh surveyed the Murrah building in December 1994 and made dozens of calls to obtain explosives.

Ryan spoke of the 160 people killed along with the eight federal officers and said McVeigh "had to kill all those innocent persons to accomplish the goal of killing these eight law enforcement officers."

He also spoke of the 19 children killed in the bombing, including 15 in a day care centre, and said McVeigh put many others at risk of death besides the 168 who died. He talked of people who had been maimed, such as Daina Bradley, who had to have her leg amputated to free her from the rubble.
Ryan said prosecutors would show a videotape of three children badly injured in the bombing as they are today.
